power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: The language used to discuss autism both reflects and shapes perceptions of Autistic people, yet research on terminology preferences has largely been confined to English.
This study examines autism-related terminology in Greek.

A sample of 1,006 Greek-speaking adults (124 Autistic adults, 434 parents/caregivers, and 448 professionals) completed an online survey, selecting, from a list of 61 terms, those they use to refer to autism, Autistic people, autism-related difficulties, and non-autistic people, and explained their choices.
Data were analysed using demographics-adjusted group comparisons, principal component analysis, and thematic analysis.

The groups shared a core vocabulary ("autism", "difficulties", "is on the autism spectrum") but differed in their use of 39 terms, with small effects, and the main contrasts persisted after demographic adjustment.

Autistic adults preferred identity-first and neurodiversity terminology, professionals favoured clinical terminology, and parents/caregivers resembled professionals on identity terms and Autistic adults on clinical terms.
Identity and clinical vocabularies were independent dimensions on which every group was represented.
Open-ended responses tied these choices to identity among Autistic adults, others' reactions among parents/caregivers, and audience and setting among professionals.
We discuss these findings in the context of autism research and their implications for practice and public discourse.
The language used to describe autism influences how Autistic people are perceived, accepted, and view themselves.

Autistic self-advocates and researchers have consistently linked language to experiences of recognition, stigma, and exclusion (Sinclair, 1999; Brown, 2011; Kapp et al., 2013; Botha et al., 2023; Botha & Cage, 2022).

text.text: Evidence from English-speaking contexts A growing body of survey research has documented the preferences for autism-related terminology.

The first large study, in the United Kingdom (Kenny et al., 2016; N = 3,470), showed that autistic was endorsed by a majority of Autistic adults and about half of parents, but by far fewer professionals.

text.text: Overall, cross-cultural studies indicate that stakeholder differences are generally consistent across contexts, but their size, and occasionally their direction, vary depending on language, instrument, and sample.
Each new language provides an opportunity to test these patterns further.

First, the word autism comes from Greek, combining εαυτός ('self') and the suffix -ισμός (Kassas et al., 2021).

text.text: Autistic people and their families continue to report uneven support and ongoing stigma.
This study offers the first systematic evidence on the language used by Greek-speaking Autistic adults, parents and caregivers, and professionals.
We examine not only which terms each group uses, but also how the groups differ when demographic factors are considered, how individuals combine different terms, and the reasons behind their choices.
We designed a brief online survey, adapted from earlier English-and French-language studies, and distributed it through community networks and P r e p r i n t social media.
Our approach combines group comparisons that account for demographic differences, person-level analysis of term combinations, and thematic analysis of participants' explanations.
This design aims to capture both the diversity of language use and the underlying reasons for these choices.

Participants were 1,006 Greek-speaking adults recruited through autism advocacy networks, professional associations, universities, community organisations, and social media in Greece, Cyprus, and Greek-speaking diaspora communities.

Inclusion criteria were being an adult, speaking Greek fluently, and belonging to one of three stakeholder groups: Autistic adults (n = 124; 78 with a formal diagnosis and 46 self-identified), parents/caregivers of Autistic people (n = 434; 394 parents or guardians of a child with a formal diagnosis, 26 of a child without one, and 14 other relatives), and professionals (n = 448; 427 practitioners, such as psychologists and special education teachers, and 21 researchers).

Participants with more than one of these identities (e.g., an Autistic parent) were allocated to the group closer to Autistic identity, and 15 respondents who belonged to none of the groups were excluded.
Most participants lived in Greece (93.5%) or Cyprus (4.0%).

The groups differed markedly in demographic profile (Supplementary Table S1): half of Autistic adults were aged 18-29, whereas four in five parents/caregivers were 40 or over; women made up 69% of Autistic adults and over 90% of the other two groups; and 51% of Autistic adults, 68% of parents/caregivers, and 94% of professionals held a university degree or higher.

Six items recorded age, gender, stakeholder group, highest level of education, country of residence, and whether Greek was the participant's first language.

Six terminology items asked which of the listed terms participants use for autism itself, for an Autistic person, for a person's diagnostic characterisation (in separate sub-questions for P r e p r i n t formulations with has and with is), for autism more broadly (as a condition, disability, disorder, and so on), for autism-related difficulties, and for a person without a diagnosis, 61 terms in all (Supplementary Table S3).

text.text: Each terminology item also had an 'other' textbox field, and a final item invited participants to explain the reasons behind their choices in a text box with no length limit.
Three features of the Greek context were reflected in the questionnaire (Supplementary Section A.2).
First, adjectives were given in their masculine, feminine, and neuter forms (αυτιστικός/ή/ό, autistic).
Second, two Greek words for neurodiversity were offered.
In νευροδιαφορετικότητα, the second constituent (διαφορετικότητα) suggests both diversity and difference, hence the translation neurodiversity/neurodivergence.
By contrast, νευροποικιλότητα (translated here as neurodiversity) is a more direct analogue of biodiversity, as it builds on its Greek equivalent, βιοποικιλότητα.

Finally, Asperger's syndrome and pervasive developmental disorder were retained because they remain in Greek diagnostic, administrative, and everyday use (Law 3699/2008; Papanikolaou & Pehlivanidis, 2025).

Participation was voluntary and unpaid.

Participants read an information page and gave electronic informed consent before proceeding; no identifying information was requested, and participants were assured that their responses were anonymous and confidential.
The survey took a median of 6 minutes to complete.
This study was designed and led by academic researchers and was not co-produced.
Community input entered at three points.

None of us identifies as Autistic.
We approached terminology use as an empirical question without treating any form as inherently correct.

In reporting the findings, we generally use identity-first language in recognition of its endorsement by many Autistic adults, while preserving participants' own terminology when describing their responses.
The study followed a convergent mixed-methods design and is reported according to the GRAMMS guidelines (O'Cathain et al., 2008).

text.text: The analysis asked three questions in turn: which terms each stakeholder group selects, and whether the differences between groups survive adjustment for their different demographic profiles; how the endorsements of the 61 terms combine within individuals; and, from the open-ended responses, how participants account for their choices.
Quantitative analyses were conducted in Python 3.13 (details in Supplementary Methods, Section A.3; data and code in the Data Availability Statement).
Term-by-term comparisons.
Each of the 61 terms was coded as selected or not selected by each participant ('other' entries were summarised separately).

For each term, the three groups were compared with a 3 × 2 chi-square test of independence, with p-values adjusted across the 61 tests by the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995; adjusted values denoted p BH , with p BH < 0.05 treated as significant).

Because the three groups differed markedly in age, gender, and education (Supplementary Table S1), the group contrasts were re-estimated with binary logistic P r e p r i n t regressions for twelve focal terms representing the framings at the centre of the terminology debate (listed in Figure 3).

Dimensions of use.
To examine how the 61 endorsements combine within individuals, we conducted a principal component analysis (PCA) of the participant × term matrix.

Whereas the term-by-term comparisons ask which group selects a term more often, PCA asks which terms tend to be selected together, summarising co-selection in a small number of dimensions on which each term receives a loading and each participant a score.
The PCA was run on the centred binary data using the covariance matrix, so that a term's influence is proportional to how often it was selected.
The number of dimensions was decided by parallel analysis, the drop in variance explained, and interpretability.
An unrotated solution is reported, oriented so that higher scores denote greater use of the vocabulary naming each dimension, and it was stable under bootstrap resampling.

We preferred the PCA-based dimensional description to an exploratory cluster analysis because, as our data included binary endorsements, the cluster solutions proved unstable (Supplementary Methods, Section A.3).
Group differences in dimension scores were tested with one-way ANOVA (η²) and Cohen's d, and re-estimated with linear regressions adjusting for age band, gender, and education.

text.text: Three terms were selected by a majority of all three groups: autism (αυτισμός; 61.3%, 56.5%, and 63.6% of Autistic adults, parents/caregivers, and professionals, respectively), difficulties (δυσκολίες; 75.0%, 71.9%, and 65.4%), and is on the autism spectrum (είναι στο φάσμα του αυτισμού; 53.2%, 63.6%, and 74.8%).
At the other extreme, disease (νόσος), illness (πάθηση), and defects (ελαττώματα) were selected by fewer than 5% of any group, so the groups shared a core vocabulary and a set of rejected terms.

text.text: Autistic adults differed from professionals on 33 of the 39 terms and from parents/caregivers on 21, whereas parents/caregivers differed from professionals on 19.
Three tendencies summarise these differences (Figure 1).
text.formatted: Three tendencies summarise these differences (Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>).

text.text: First, Autistic adults selected neurodiversity and identity-first terms far more often than parents/caregivers and professionals, for example neurodiversity (νευροποικιλότητα; 32.3% vs 7.1% and 11.6%, respectively), neurodivergent person (νευροδιαφορετικό άτομο; 43.5% vs 19.1% and 18.3%), autistic (αυτιστικός/ή/ό; 52.4% vs 32.3% and 29.5%), and, for a person without a diagnosis, non-autistic (27.4% vs 7.4% and 8.3%); on these terms, parents/caregivers and professionals were indistinguishable.
Second, professionals selected clinical and diagnostic terminology substantially more often than the other two groups.

Examples include has an ASD diagnosis (έχει διάγνωση ΔΑΦ; 18.5%, 25.8%, and 51.8% of Autistic adults, parents/caregivers, and professionals, respectively), autism spectrum disorder (22.6%, 24.0%, and 48.0%), deficits (ελλείμματα; 13.7%, 20.7%, and 41.1%), and disorder (διαταραχή; 31.5%, 41.9%, and 62.1%).
For these terms, parents/caregivers showed patterns of endorsement more similar to those of Autistic adults.
Third, parents/caregivers did not consistently occupy a middle ground between the other two groups.
Their endorsement levels were broadly comparable to those of professionals for neurodiversity and identity-first terms, and to those of Autistic adults for clinical and diagnostic terms.

This pattern of alternating alignment was also evident for Asperger's syndrome, which parents/caregivers endorsed P r e p r i n t at levels closer to those of Autistic adults (38.7%, 31.3%, and 19.9% of Autistic adults, parents/caregivers, and professionals, respectively), and for functioning labels, which they endorsed more frequently than Autistic adults and at levels closer to those of professionals (36.3%, 50.5%, and 59.8%, respectively).

text.text: Among professionals, the balance was reversed (36.2% vs 60.5%), whereas parents/caregivers leaned neither way (35.9% vs 34.8%) and were the group most likely to select neither framing (38.9%) and to rely on spectrum phrasing alone (33.4%).

For parents/caregivers, as for professionals, the single most selected term for an Autistic person was person on the autism spectrum (50.5% and 55.6%, vs 41.1% of Autistic adults), whereas for Autistic adults it was autistic (52.4%).

The two framings were not mutually exclusive, as 15.3% of Autistic adults and 19.4% of professionals selected both, and neurodiversity terms were selected by half of Autistic adults (49.2%) but by only a quarter of parents/caregivers (28.6%) and professionals (25.9%).

Professionals, but not parents/caregivers, also had higher odds of selecting autism spectrum disorder (OR = 3.75 [2.21, 6.38]), person with autism (OR = 2.80 [1.66, 4.71]), and deficits (OR = 2.98 [1.66, 5.37]).

Neither group differed from Autistic adults on autism or disability, and the lower selection of autistic person by parents/caregivers was no longer significant after adjustment (OR = 0.59 [0.31, 1.14]).
Age, gender, and education had modest associations with the selection of individual terms (Supplementary Results, Section B.1).
Within the Autistic group, formally diagnosed (n = 78) and self-identified (n = 46) adults selected identity-first terms at the same rate (56.4% vs 54.3%).

Diagnosed adults were, however, twice as likely to also select person-first terms (43.6% vs 21.7%, p = 0.014; adjusted OR = 2.41 [1.01, 5.79]) and half as likely to select neurodiversity (νευροποικιλότητα; 24.4% vs 45.7%, p = 0.014; adjusted OR = 0.43 [0.19, 0.99]).

The third dimension (6.7%) is bipolar, contrasting terms that name autism without using the P r e p r i n t word itself (the neurodiversity terms, Asperger's syndrome, neurotypical person) with the plain autism words (autism, autistic, is autistic, has autism).

As at term level, then, parents/caregivers resembled professionals on the identity dimension and Autistic adults on the clinical dimension.

text.text: Three concerns ran through all three groups, autism as difference, the stigma attached to autistic (αυτιστικός), and the sources of one's vocabulary, each approached from the group's own position.

text.text: Professionals approached terminology through the demands of different settings.

They described autism as a difference [Pr-10], emphasised respecting individual preferences ('it is not for us, as neurotypical people, to decide the "correct" terminology' [Pr-1426]), and sought to avoid stigmatising language.
Some did so by choosing words carefully when speaking with children [Pr-1428], while others used autistic openly to challenge its negative connotations .

text.text: Many adapted their terminology to their audience, using on the autism spectrum with parents who might not be ready to hear autistic [Pr-1529], and clinical terms such as disorder with colleagues .

text.text: Others drew on diagnostic manuals and clinical training [Pr-541] or followed the terminology preferred by the Autistic community.

Taken together, these accounts suggest that terminology choices reflect considerations of identity, anticipated stigma, disability, and communicative context, rather than fixed preferences associated with stakeholder group.
This study provides, to our knowledge, the first systematic evidence on autism-related terminology use in Greek, based on responses from 1,006 Autistic adults, parents/caregivers, and professionals.
Our analysis produced four main findings.

First, all three groups converged on a core set of terms (autism, difficulties, is on the autism spectrum) and rarely selected strongly negative terms, but differed in their use of 39 of the 61 terms examined.
These differences were generally small, and the main contrasts persisted after adjustment for age, gender, and education.
Second, the pattern of differences broadly resembled that reported in English-language research.
Autistic adults selected identity-first and neurodiversity-related terms more often, whereas professionals selected clinical and diagnostic terminology more often.

Parents/caregivers did not consistently occupy an intermediate position, instead aligning with professionals on identity-related terminology and with Autistic adults on clinical terms, with person on the autism spectrum as their most frequently selected expression.
Third, identity-related and clinical vocabularies emerged as independent dimensions rather than opposite ends of a single continuum.
All three groups were represented across combinations of these dimensions, and stakeholder group membership accounted for less than a tenth of the variance in either score.

Fourth, open-ended responses revealed concerns shared across groups, including the understanding of autism as a difference, the stigma associated with autistic, and the influences shaping terminology choices.
These concerns were articulated from different perspectives, reflecting identity, caregiving experience, and professional expectations.

Identity-first language was therefore more frequently endorsed, but without a clear consensus.
The Greek findings also bear on the Dutch exception, where most Autistic adults (Buijsman et al., 2023; De Laet et al., 2025) and parents (Buijsman et al., 2023) favour person-first language.

text.text: Two explanations have been proposed.

One concerns cultural traditions that downplay difference (Buijsman et al., 2023), while the other, offered more tentatively, points to the stigmatising connotations of the Dutch identity-first term (De Laet et al., 2025).

text.text: The Greek findings complicate a purely stigma-based explanation.
In Greek, too, the identity-first term (the bare adjective αυτιστικός) was reported by participants to be used as an insult, yet Greek Autistic adults more frequently selected identity-first forms.
Qualitative accounts revealed contrasting responses to this stigma, as some participants avoided the word, whereas others deliberately used it to challenge its derogatory connotations.

The French evidence points the same way, as autiste is also reported to be used as an insult, yet French-speaking Autistic adults favour identity-first forms (Fecteau et al., 2024; Geelhand et al., 2023).
text.formatted: The French evidence points the same way, as autiste is also reported to be used as an insult, yet French-speaking Autistic adults favour identity-first forms <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Fecteau et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Geelhand et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, the presence of stigma alone does not appear to determine whether identity-first or person-first language predominates, although the intensity and social meanings of stigma cannot be directly compared across the two languages.
The most frequently selected identity-first constructions were the bare adjective and the copular form rather than the noun phrase.
Among Autistic adults, autistic (52%) and is autistic (61%) were selected considerably more often than autistic person (20%), and the adjective also outranked the noun phrase in the other two groups.
This ordering is not universal.

French-speaking Autistic adults endorsed the noun phrase personne autiste (72%) about as often as autiste (67%) and est autiste (81%; Geelhand et al., 2023), and English-speaking Autistic adults endorsed autistic person at 80% (Keating et al., 2023).

text.text: These findings suggest that restricting identity-first language to noun phrases may underestimate its use, particularly in languages where adjectival constructions are common.

That said, although the Greek case was motivated partly on linguistic grounds, including transparent etymology, a morphology that allows the adjective to stand alone, and a predominantly person-first official vocabulary, participants often explained their choices in sociocultural terms.

Concerns about the term for autistic (αυτιστικός/ή/ό) centred on its derogatory use rather than its grammatical form, while terminology choices were influenced by professionals, diagnostic manuals, and the Autistic community, often encountered online.
Linguistic structures may therefore shape the available forms, while awareness, stigma, community identification, and trusted sources influence which are adopted.
The most pronounced differences between Autistic adults and the other groups lay not in the identity-first versus person-first distinction but in neurodiversity-related vocabulary.
Neurodiversity (νευροποικιλότητα, 32% vs 7-12%), neurodivergent person (44% vs 18-19%), and the contrastive term non-autistic (27% vs 7-8%) were selected considerably more often by Autistic adults.
Self-identified Autistic adults selected νευροποικιλότητα at twice the rate of those with a formal diagnosis, a difference that persisted after adjustment for age band and gender.

Of the two Greek renderings of neurodiversity, νευροδιαφορετικότητα was used more widely across stakeholder groups, with approximately half of parents/caregivers and professionals selecting it, whereas νευροποικιλότητα remained largely concentrated among Autistic adults.
This pattern is consistent with the broader uptake of neurodiversity language among neurodivergent adults (Pearson et al., 2026).

text.text: The third principal component distinguished direct autism terminology from alternative labels, including neurodiversity-related terms and Asperger's syndrome.

Qualitative accounts of avoiding autistic offer one possible interpretation of some of these endorsement patterns, although the component may also reflect other distinctions, including identity, diagnostic history, and perceived accuracy.
The quantitative patterns were also consistent with themes in the qualitative responses.
Autistic adults scored higher on the identity and neurodiversity dimension, whereas professionals scored higher on the clinical-diagnostic dimension.
Nevertheless, substantial variation remained within each group, consistent with findings from other contexts (Dwyer et al., 2026; Lao et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Nevertheless, substantial variation remained within each group, consistent with findings from other contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Dwyer et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Lao et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Professionals' qualitative responses suggested that clinical terminology often reflected diagnostic conventions and professional contexts rather than necessarily indicating opposition to identity-first language.

Many P r e p r i n t emphasised that the appropriate term is the one preferred by the Autistic person, and several noted that it is not for neurotypical professionals to determine the correct terminology.
The alternating alignment of parents/caregivers with the other two stakeholder groups is one of the clearer findings in our study.
Mixed alignment among parents is not specific to Greek.

In French-speaking Canada, parents rated autistic, autistic person, and person with ASD about equally, whereas Autistic adults favoured the first two and professionals the third (Fecteau et al., 2024).
text.formatted: In French-speaking Canada, parents rated autistic, autistic person, and person with ASD about equally, whereas Autistic adults favoured the first two and professionals the third <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Fecteau et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In the United Kingdom, parents rarely endorsed person with autism deviating frm profressionals, yet over half described their child with has autism, similarly to professionals (Kenny et al., 2016).
text.formatted: In the United Kingdom, parents rarely endorsed person with autism deviating frm profressionals, yet over half described their child with has autism, similarly to professionals <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Kenny et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: The open-ended responses help explain this pattern.
Some parents/caregivers, like some Autistic adults, resisted disorder and deficit terminology because they regarded it as pathologising a child they understood as different rather than ill.
At the same time, some avoided autistic because of anticipated negative reactions, favouring person on the autism spectrum as a less stigmatising alternative.
Others, particularly those describing lifelong support needs, considered disability and disorder more accurate.
Consistent with this variation, 42% of parents/caregivers selected disorder, compared with 32% of Autistic adults and 62% of professionals.
Their terminology choices also reflected potentially competing influences, including professionals involved in supporting their children and the Autistic community.
For some parents/caregivers, anticipated stigma thus had immediate implications for how they described their children.

Their accounts highlight the potential importance of public education in challenging the derogatory associations of αυτιστικός, while also showing why terminology choices cannot be reduced to a single parental perspective.

For practice in Greek-speaking settings, the findings support the principle emphasised in English-language research: to ask about and respect the individual's terminology preferences (Keating et al., 2023).

text.text: This principle was also endorsed by professionals in our study.

Where individual preferences cannot be established, we take the view, consistent with Dwyer (2022) and Schuck et al. (2025), that the preferences of Autistic adults should carry greater weight than those of parents/caregivers or professionals, because the terminology concerns Autistic people themselves.

(2025)</ref>, that the preferences of Autistic adults should carry greater weight than those of parents/caregivers or professionals, because the terminology concerns Autistic people themselves.

text.text: On this basis, the Greek findings support three more specific recommendations.

First, where individual preferences are unknown, Greek-language guidance should give particular consideration to is autistic (είναι αυτιστικός/ή/ό, 61%) and the bare adjective autistic (52%), the identity-first forms most frequently selected by Autistic adults in this study.
At the same time, is on the autism spectrum, selected by a majority in every group (53%, 64%, and 75%), offers widely used terminology for communication across stakeholder groups.

Second, the contrast between has and is, raised unprompted by participants in all three groups (Supplementary Table S4), suggests that Greek-language guidance should address predicate constructions as well as noun phrases when discussing identity-first and person-first language.
text.formatted: Second, the contrast between has and is, raised unprompted by participants in all three groups (Supplementary Table <ref type="table">S4</ref>), suggests that Greek-language guidance should address predicate constructions as well as noun phrases when discussing identity-first and person-first language.

text.text: In particular, is autistic (είναι αυτιστικός/ή/ό) deserves consideration alongside autistic person (αυτιστικό άτομο), rather than treating the noun phrase as the sole identity-first form.

Third, the stigma attached to autistic (αυτιστικός) in everyday Greek (see also Papoudi & Antonopoulou, 2025; Zarokanellou et al., 2024b Zarokanellou et al., , 2025)), which contributed to avoidance among some parents/caregivers and professionals, is a matter of public discourse rather than terminology alone.

text.text: Media language both reflects and may influence attitudes towards autism (Karaminis et al., 2023; Dickinson & Karaminis, 2026).
text.formatted: Media language both reflects and may influence attitudes towards autism <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Karaminis et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Dickinson & Karaminis, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The media, as well as educational institutions, therefore have a potential role in challenging the derogatory associations of this word, as some Autistic adults in our study already sought to do through its deliberate use.

Limitations and future directions Our sample, recruited through advocacy and professional networks, was predominantly female and highly educated, with Autistic adults who were mostly young and, in approximately one-third of cases, self-identified.
Recruitment through these networks, together with voluntary participation, may have attracted respondents with a particular interest in autism-related terminology.
The endorsement percentages should therefore not be treated as population estimates.

Autistic people with intellectual disabilities or those who do not communicate in writing were also likely to be under-represented, consistent with broader limitations in the literature (Schuck et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Autistic people with intellectual disabilities or those who do not communicate in writing were also likely to be under-represented, consistent with broader limitations in the literature <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Schuck et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, the terminology patterns observed among participating Autistic adults should not be assumed to represent all Autistic people.
Future research will require alternative survey formats and appropriate involvement of supporters to include a wider range of communication and support needs.
The study measured which terms participants reported using, rather than their attitudes towards those terms.
Infrequently selected terms may therefore be tolerated rather than actively rejected, and the survey did not include a 'no preference' option.
Future studies should combine terminology selection with ratings of liking and perceived offensiveness (Bury et al., 2023a; Pearson et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Future studies should combine terminology selection with ratings of liking and perceived offensiveness <ref type="bibr">(Bury et al., 2023a;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Pearson et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: They should also consider terms suggested in the 'other' fields, including typically developing (τυπικής ανάπτυξης), support needs, allistic (αλλιστικός), autistic neurotype, and social-model expressions such as barriers and lack of accommodations.
The study was designed and led by academic researchers rather than co-produced with the Autistic community.

Although community members contributed through piloting, recruitment, and discussions of preliminary findings, a stronger participatory approach involving Greek-speaking Autistic people in questionnaire development, analysis, and interpretation would help address this limitation (Karaminis et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Although community members contributed through piloting, recruitment, and discussions of preliminary findings, a stronger participatory approach involving Greek-speaking Autistic people in questionnaire development, analysis, and interpretation would help address this limitation <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Karaminis et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, stakeholder-group differences were generally small, and the three components interpreted here accounted for approximately one-quarter of the variance in term endorsements.
Four additional components exceeded chance levels but were not examined in detail, leaving other dimensions of terminology use to be explored.
The findings also represent a snapshot from 2024-2025 of a vocabulary that continues to evolve, highlighting the value of repeated surveys.

Greek-speaking Autistic adults, parents/caregivers, and professionals shared a core autism-related vocabulary but differed in their use of identity-first, neurodiversity-related, and clinical terminology, broadly reflecting patterns reported in English and French.
These group differences coexisted with substantial variation within groups, and identity-related and clinical vocabularies emerged as independent dimensions.
Qualitative accounts showed how terminology choices reflected identity, anticipated stigma, caregiving experiences, and professional context.
The findings support giving greater weight to Autistic adults' terminology preferences in Greek-language guidance while respecting individual choices.
They also highlight the importance of challenging the stigma associated with αυτιστικός, rather than allowing its derogatory use to determine how Autistic people are described.
